standard.title: Language, expressions and gestures
standard.description: understand how language, facial expressions and gestures are used to interact with others when asking for and providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore how language is used differently at home and school depending on relationships and contexts (AC9EFLA01). They have not yet understood the specific functions of language, facial expressions and gestures across distinct interaction types such as requesting, exclaiming, and commanding.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how language, facial expressions and gestures work together across different types of interaction — providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands.

nodes.label: Communication is multimodal
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that communication involves more than words — gestures, facial expressions and body language all carry meaning.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two non-verbal communication modes (e.g. gesture, facial expression) and explain that they contribute meaning alongside words.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and discuss how words, facial expressions, gestures and body language each contribute to meaning in everyday interactions, including in short film or picture book examples.
wider: Explore how symbols and body language function as primary communication modes in First Nations Australian communities, comparing with verbal-dominant communication
Investigate how meaning changes when body language and words send conflicting signals (e.g. saying 'fine' while frowning)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who equate communication with speech only cannot engage with N4's analysis of how language, expression and gesture combine — the multimodal frame is definitionally required before the combination can be examined.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate communication with speech only. Encountering diverse multimodal examples — film, picture books, First Nations contexts — helps build the understanding that non-verbal modes carry independent meaning, not just accompaniment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations communication systems offer a culturally significant and pedagogically rich context for exploring non-verbal meaning-making that goes well beyond typical classroom examples.
success_criteria: Student names at least two non-verbal communication modes and gives an example of each
Student explains that gestures or facial expressions can change how a message is received

nodes.label: Interaction types have distinct features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different types of interaction — providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting, giving commands — and recognise that each uses different language.
nodes.minimum_width: Name and give an example of at least three interaction types (e.g. asking a question, giving a command, making an offer).
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss the full range of interaction types from the descriptor, recognising differences in language and tone across providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands.
wider: Compare how the same interaction type (e.g. requesting) sounds different in formal versus informal contexts
Identify interaction types in short film clips and discuss how character relationships affect language choices

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a working set of interaction type examples — the learning is in recognising the range, not in any single instance. More examples across varied contexts build the category.

success_criteria: Student correctly names and gives an example of at least three different interaction types
Student identifies how the language used differs between at least two interaction types

nodes.label: Open and closed questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between open and closed questions and understand that question type shapes the kind of response expected.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a given question is open or closed and explain what kind of answer each invites.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish open questions (inviting extended response) from closed questions (yes/no or single answer), give examples of each, and discuss how question choice affects conversation.
wider: Explore how open questions are used in discussions to invite opinion versus closed questions used to check facts
Investigate how question type shifts in different interaction contexts — classroom discussion, playground, storytelling

response_modes.reason: Students frequently confuse open/closed question distinction in practice. Repeated sorting and labelling of examples builds the precision needed to reliably apply the distinction.

success_criteria: Student correctly classifies a given question as open or closed
Student explains what kind of response an open question invites versus a closed question

nodes.label: Language, expression and gesture work together
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how language choices, facial expressions and gestures combine to shape how an interaction is received by others.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how a speaker's words and body language together affect how their message is received in at least one interaction type.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the combination of language, facial expression and gesture shapes meaning across multiple interaction types, using examples from texts or familiar situations.
wider: Discuss how the same verbal request can be received differently depending on facial expression and tone — e.g. a polite request vs an impatient demand
Explore representations of interaction in literature by First Nations Australian authors, discussing how visual and verbal elements together create meaning

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate their understanding of verbal and non-verbal modes together — it's not adding new content but assembling the components from nodes 1–3 into a unified explanation of how communication works.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The combination node is rich for advancing students — exploring how meaning shifts when modes align versus conflict, and examining how First Nations authors represent this in literature, offers genuine interpretive depth.
success_criteria: Student gives an example showing how body language and words together affect how a message is received
Student explains, for at least one interaction type, how changing the gesture or expression would change the meaning
